title: Application Organization and Naming
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of application organization and naming and at least two listed subtopics.
Interpret the application organization and naming example and predict its expected result.
Choose a verification step and identify one version, security, data, or troubleshooting consideration.

content.intro: Learn application organization and naming through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Application Organization and Naming matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines application organization and naming as part of django project structure and configuration. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: App naming conventions; Keeping responsibilities focused; Cross-app dependencies; Python package imports; Avoiding circular imports. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Change one input or configuration choice related to App naming conventions. Write down the expected outcome, test one normal case and one invalid or boundary case, then record what changed. Do not add real credentials or sensitive production data.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a framework fragment without its imports, configuration, model, or URL context.
common_mistakes.why: The snippet may be incomplete when separated from a Django project.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the stated prerequisites and run the relevant management check or focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting input or relying only on a happy-path example.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid values, unauthorized requests, or concurrent activity can violate assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and add a negative or boundary test.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating the development sample as production-ready.
common_mistakes.why: Production hosting, secrets, storage, monitoring and resource limits differ from local use.
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the current deployment/security references and document untested areas.
